questions.question: At duration $t$, every policy in a cohort has ended, so the in-force event $I$ has probability zero. A cohort variable $W$ is set to zero for ended policies. Does $E[W]=0$ establish an active-policy prospective value at $t$?
options: Yes: zero cohort outgo establishes zero conditional liability.
No: ordinary conditioning on the event $I$ is undefined here.
Yes: zero-filling uniquely determines the mean within $I$.
No: the earlier premium amounts are needed to condition on $I$.

questions.question: An active policy has prospective value 20 on a specified valuation basis. What interpretation is justified by that number alone?
options: Every future loss scenario is no larger than 20.
The maximum remaining nominal benefit is exactly 20.
Expected discounted future costs exceed premium income by 20.
Future outgo equals future income plus 20 on every lifetime.

questions.question: A policy is evaluated at duration $t=4$ years. Which cash-flow valuation corresponds to its prospective policy value at that date?
options: Expected remaining costs minus income, discounted to duration 4.
Accumulated past benefits minus past premiums at duration 4.
Expected remaining costs minus income, discounted to policy issue.
Expected total lifetime costs minus total lifetime income, including past flows.

questions.question: An active policy has benefit PV $Z$ and unit future premium-stream PV $U$, with finite conditional expectations on its valuation basis. Its net level premium is $P_n$ and gross premium is $P_g$, with $P_g>P_n>0$ and positive unit-stream APV. Which expression defines its net prospective value for every such contract when expenses are omitted?
options: $E[Z\mid\text{in force}]-P_gE[U\mid\text{in force}]$
$P_nE[U\mid\text{in force}]-E[Z\mid\text{in force}]$
$E[Z\mid\text{in force}]+P_nE[U\mid\text{in force}]$
$E[Z\mid\text{in force}]-P_nE[U\mid\text{in force}]$

questions.question: A contract has fixed level premium $P$ chosen on its original pricing basis. An actuary now changes the basis used to calculate its prospective value, without altering the contract terms. What should happen to $P$ in that valuation?
options: Reprice $P$ automatically so that the new policy value is zero.
Keep $P$ fixed and recalculate the expected future cash flows on the new basis.
Drop all future premium income because $P$ came from another basis.
Keep all old cost and income APVs because $P$ is fixed.

questions.question: For an active policy, expected current-origin PV of remaining benefits and expenses is 58, and expected current-origin PV of remaining premiums is 35. What is its prospective gross value?
Conditional on being in force at duration $t$, a policy has gross future loss -10 with probability 0.75 and 50 with probability 0.25, both valued at $t$. What is its prospective value?

At a policy valuation date, expected remaining benefit PV is 90, expected remaining expense PV is 12, and the unit future premium-stream APV is 10, all conditional on being in force. The contractual level premium is 8. What is prospective gross value?
For an active policy, expected remaining benefit PV is 20 and expected remaining premium-income PV is 30. There are no expenses. Which statement about net prospective value is correct?
options: It equals 10, representing expected future benefit costs above income.
It equals -10, representing expected future income above benefit costs.
It equals zero because a policy value cannot be negative.
It equals 50 because both remaining cash-flow streams have positive APVs.

questions.question: A policy has prospective gross value 18. Its contract is revised to add one fixed future expense with current APV 5; all other future cash flows and the valuation basis remain unchanged. What is the revised value?

Let $I$ be the event that a policy is in force at duration $t$, with $0<P(I)<1$. Its integrable current future loss is $L_t$ on $I$, and prospective value is $V_t=E[L_t\mid I]$. Define an original-cohort variable $W$ equal to $L_t$ on $I$ and zero on the complement $I^c$. Which identity recovers $V_t$ for every such model?
options: $V_t=E[W]$
$V_t=P(I)E[W]$
$V_t=E[W]/P(I)$
$V_t=E[W]/P(I^c)$

questions.question: For an active policy, let $Z,H,Y$ be integrable current PVs of future benefits, expenses and premium income. Prospective gross value is $V=E[Z+H-Y\mid\text{in force}]$. Beyond integrability, which relationship between those three cash-flow values is needed to split this into their three conditional expectations?
options: They must be mutually independent conditional on being in force.
The covariance of total future costs and premium income must be zero.
Benefit and premium payments must occur on disjoint events.
No extra independence or covariance condition is needed.

questions.question: For a policy in force, prospective gross value immediately before receiving a premium due now is 12. The premium is 6 and its collection expense is 1.5, both presently unpaid and included among future cash flows. Later cash flows and the valuation basis are fixed. What is the value immediately after both flows are settled?

An active portfolio contains 200 policies of group A, each with prospective value 50, and 800 of group B, each with value -5 on a common valuation basis. A policy is selected uniformly from these 1000 active policies. What is its expected prospective value?

At one valuation date, a policy has expected remaining benefit PV 50 and unit premium-stream APV 10. Its net premium is 4 and gross premium is 6. Expected remaining gross expense PV is 15. On the same basis, which comparison of corresponding net and gross prospective values holds?
options: Net value is 10; gross value is 25, so the gross value is larger.
Net value is 10; gross value is -25, so the gross value is smaller.
Net value is 10; gross value is 15, so the gross value is larger.
Net value is 10; gross value is 5, so the gross value is smaller.

questions.question: An original policy cohort has duration-2 outcomes: probability 0.5 of a policy already ended, probability 0.1 of an active policy with future loss 40, and probability 0.4 of an active policy with future loss -5. What is the prospective value for an active duration-2 policy?

At zero interest and without expenses, a policy pays 100 at duration 2 only to lives surviving duration 1; such survivors all reach duration 2. Half survive duration 1. It collects an issue premium $P$ and 50 at duration 1 from survivors. Which issue-equivalence premium and prospective value just before that later receipt are correct?
options: Issue premium 50; active duration 1 value 0.
Issue premium 25; active duration 1 value 50.
Issue premium 25; active duration 1 value-50.
Issue premium 50; active duration 1 value 50.

questions.question: For an active policy, current future benefit PV $Z$ and premium-income PV $Y$ both equal the same non-negative random amount $W$, finite on every scenario but with $E[W]=+\infty$ on the active-policy basis. Expenses are zero. Prospective value is defined through the conditional mean of loss $L=Z-Y$. Which statement is valid?
options: $V=0$, because the loss $L=W-W$ is zero on every scenario.
$V$ is undefined because each component APV is infinite.
$V=+\infty$ because expected benefits are infinite.
$V=-\infty$ because expected premium income is infinite.

questions.question: Conditional on being in force, a policy future loss is -20 with probability 0.5, 80 with probability 0.4, and 180 with probability 0.1. A fund equal to its prospective value is held at the same date. What is the probability that future loss exceeds that fund?

For active policies with zero expenses, both future benefit PV $Z$ and premium-income PV $Y$ take 0 or 100 with equal marginal probabilities. Model A assigns joint pairs $(Z,Y)=(0,0),(100,100)$ equally. Model B assigns $(0,100),(100,0)$ equally. Which comparison of prospective values and positive-loss probabilities is correct?
options: Both values are 0; positive-loss probability is 0 in both models.
The values differ because the dependence of benefits and premiums differs.
Both values are 0; positive-loss probability is $1/4$ in both models.
Both values are 0; positive-loss probabilities are 0 in A and $1/2$ in B.
